title: The Confidence of Stretching Others
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article makes the case for stretch assignments as a developmental tool, while cautioning that simply throwing someone into a challenge without conversation can backfire. It compares giving people new responsibilities before they feel fully ready to teaching someone to swim or ride a bike, where growth depends on a more experienced person's guidance and confidence. The piece recommends an explicit conversation before the assignment begins, in which a leader explains specifically why they believe the person is ready, rather than assuming intent is obvious. It argues that this conversation, more than the assignment itself, often becomes the most memorable and motivating moment for the team member. The archivist notes this piece complements other Admired Leadership essays on delegation and talent development.
points: Stretch assignments accelerate growth, but most people meet them with trepidation rather than eagerness.
Leaders should explicitly explain why they believe a team member is ready, rather than just assigning the task.
Exploring the team member's own doubts before the assignment surfaces real reservations a leader can address.
The conversation explaining a leader's confidence often outlasts and outweighs the assignment itself in impact.
Many leaders under-communicate their true judgment of a team member's talents, missing a key motivational opportunity.
quotes: But it is exactly those stretch assignments that prove our potential and accelerate our learning.
Few people are fully ready to learn how to ride a bike or to swim, so they need the confidence of someone more experienced to push them and guide them toward success.
Just throwing people into the pool or on top of the metaphorical bike sounds like a good idea, but it can actually derail success.
By exploring what the team member believes about their skills and talents relative to the assignment, leaders can appreciate whatever real reservations are in play.
Sometimes, this conversation does more to galvanize the belief team members have in themselves than does the actual assignment itself.
Months or years later, it is this conversation that remains the most powerful inspiration.
